paragraphs: Classification measures such as precision, F-measure, and G-mean summarize patterns of correct and incorrect predictions across examples. Improving them is difficult because their values generally cannot be split into separate contributions that can each be optimized independently. This paper studies how to maximize such measures when examples arrive sequentially, extending a problem studied extensively in batch learning into the online setting.

The authors introduce a general algorithm whose prediction and update rules support binary, multiclass, and multilabel classification. Its rules are computationally efficient and do not require retaining earlier examples. This makes the contribution relevant to sequential learning, where repeatedly revisiting an accumulated dataset would undermine the appeal of an online procedure.

For metrics that are both concave and smooth, the authors prove a regret rate of O(ln n / n). Those conditions matter: the stated guarantee does not cover every possible confusion-matrix metric. Empirical studies also support the algorithm’s efficiency, complementing the theoretical analysis with evidence about its practical behavior.
icml-2024-a-general-online-algorithm-for.tldr: A simple online classification algorithm optimizes complex performance metrics without storing past data, with regret guarantees for smooth, concave metrics.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization helps scientists choose which molecules to investigate by combining predictions with uncertainty about those predictions. Language models might contribute useful scientific knowledge, but the paper questions whether that knowledge actually improves a principled Bayesian search. In particular, it distinguishes Bayesian uncertainty from estimates obtained using language models that provide point estimates without a Bayesian treatment.

The authors investigate two routes for incorporating language models. One uses a model as a fixed feature extractor, passing its representations into established Bayesian optimization surrogate models. The other combines parameter-efficient fine-tuning with Bayesian neural networks to obtain a posterior for the language-model surrogate. Both approaches connect language-model representations to an explicitly Bayesian prediction framework.

Experiments on real-world chemistry problems find that language models can help molecular Bayesian optimization, but only when pretrained or fine-tuned with domain-specific data in the settings studied. The result makes domain preparation central to the reported benefit. General language-model capability alone does not establish the usefulness of a surrogate for this scientific search task.
icml-2024-a-sober-look-at-llms-for-mater.tldr: Experiments find that language models help Bayesian optimization over molecules only when they receive domain-specific pretraining or fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Searching for useful catalysts involves determining how an adsorbed molecule should sit on a surface. A typical workflow first places the molecule and then optimizes the resulting configuration toward lower energy. The initial placement therefore matters to the search. Earlier approaches have used heuristics, specialized intuition, or brute force to choose where the molecule goes and how it is oriented.

AdsorbDiff uses denoising diffusion to predict a site and orientation intended to lead to the lowest-energy configuration. The authors evaluate this placement model within a complete pipeline: a pretrained machine-learning force field optimizes the predicted configuration, and Density Functional Theory provides the final evaluation. This tests placement in conjunction with the subsequent optimization process.

The reported results show up to fivefold acceleration or a 3.5-fold improvement in accuracy relative to the previous best approach. These are qualified outcomes, rather than a claim that both gains occur together in every case. The study also examines pretraining and architecture choices, helping explain how this diffusion-based placement framework behaves.
icml-2024-adsorbdiff-adsorbate-placement.tldr: AdsorbDiff predicts molecular placements on catalyst surfaces, reporting up to fivefold acceleration or 3.5-fold better accuracy than the previous best approach.

paragraphs: Audio Flamingo addresses how to give a language model useful understanding of audio, including sounds that are not spoken words and nonverbal aspects of speech. The intended capability extends beyond extracting text from a recording. The model must also use audio information when responding to a user, adapting to a task, and participating in an ongoing conversation.

The paper combines architecture choices, training techniques, and data strategies to develop three abilities: audio understanding, adaptation to unseen tasks, and mult turn dialogue. Adaptation uses in-context learning and retrieval, allowing examples and retrieved information to help guide the model on tasks it has not previously encountered. Dialogue capability makes audio understanding part of a continuing exchange.

Evaluations across multiple audio-understanding tasks report state-of-the-art results and support the effectiveness of the overall approach. The contribution is the combination of these capabilities within an audio-language model. Its findings support the tested methods for connecting audio understanding, task adaptation, and conversation, without establishing that every unfamiliar audio task will be handled equally well.
icml-2024-audio-flamingo-a-novel-audio-l.tldr: Audio Flamingo combines audio understanding, adaptation through examples and retrieval, and ongoing dialogue, with state-of-the-art results across evaluated audio tasks.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning can produce useful representations through several different training losses, yet it is not always clear how their preferred solutions differ. This paper compares families of these losses at the level of individual batches and their asymptotic expected objectives. Under specified conditions, the authors prove that these formulations share the same minimizers.

The analysis connects those solutions to arranging representations on a hypersphere through energy minimization. This motivates Decoupled Hyperspherical Energy Loss, which separates the energy objective from the alignment of positive examples while retaining the theoretical guarantees. The separation makes the two aims easier to distinguish within the training objective.

The authors extend the results to kernel contrastive learning, whose expected loss has the additional property of being independent of batch size. This permits identification of minimizers without relying on an asymptotic regime. Computer-vision experiments report better downstream performance, greater robustness across batch sizes and hyperparameters, and less dimensionality collapse. The empirical findings complement the conditional equivalence results rather than making all contrastive losses universally interchangeable.
icml-2024-bridging-mini-batch-and-asympt.tldr: A conditional analysis links contrastive losses through hyperspherical energy and motivates objectives with improved empirical performance and reduced dimensionality collapse.

paragraphs: Language-model generation usually proceeds sequentially, which limits how much token prediction can be parallelized. Jacobi decoding reorganizes generation into repeated updates that are more amenable to parallel computation. Its practical difficulty is that an update rarely predicts more than one token correctly, so the theoretical opportunity for parallelism translates into little speed improvement.

The paper addresses this difficulty by refining the language model itself. Training encourages it to predict the final fixed point from intermediate states along a Jacobi trajectory. A fixed point is the settled result of the iterative decoding process. Encouraging agreement with that result is intended to reduce how many updates are needed to reach it.

Experiments report generation speeds 2.4 to 3.4 times higher while preserving generation quality across domain-specific and open-domain benchmarks. These results support consistency training as a way to make parallelizable decoding practically useful. The central idea is to train for rapid convergence of the decoding process, connecting the model’s learned behavior directly to the efficiency of inference.
icml-2024-cllms-consistency-large-langua.tldr: Consistency training makes Jacobi decoding converge faster, delivering reported generation speedups of 2.4–3.4 times while preserving quality.

paragraphs: An autoencoder can compress data without necessarily exploiting the structure that should make those data easier to compress. This paper makes that distinction precise for one-bit compression of sparse Gaussian data. In the shallow setting studied, the authors prove that gradient descent reaches a solution whose performance is the same as for a Gaussian source without sparsity.

For more general distributions, the authors provide evidence that the form of the learned solution changes at a critical sparsity level. Below that level, the minimizer behaves like a uniformly random rotation; above it, the minimizer becomes the identity up to a permutation. This broader transition is presented as evidence, distinct from the proved sparse-Gaussian result.

The paper then uses a connection to approximate message passing to improve compression. Adding a denoising function to a shallow architecture provably lowers the loss, and a suitable deeper decoder improves it further. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and MNIST validate the findings. The contribution connects architectural choices to whether compression can actually benefit from sparse structure.
icml-2024-compression-of-structured-data.tldr: For the studied sparse-data compression problem, shallow autoencoders can ignore sparsity, while denoising nonlinearities and suitable decoder depth provably improve performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies forecasting a measured function of the state of a discrete ergodic dynamical system over many time steps. Koopman and transfer operators provide a mathematical way to advance such functions through time. However, estimates of those operators can become unreliable when repeatedly applied, making long-term forecasting difficult even when the underlying operator framework is appropriate.

The authors improve standard estimators using eigenvalue deflation and feature centering. They also develop a technique for bounding powers of estimated operators with high probability. Powers matter because a forecast many steps ahead repeatedly applies the estimated evolution rule, so controlling a single application does not by itself establish long-horizon reliability.

Using stability theory for non-normal operators, the analysis establishes forecasting-error bounds that hold uniformly over time, including infinite horizons. The approach also supports forecasting future state distributions from an initial distribution with uniform error guarantees. Numerical experiments illustrate practical benefits. These are bounded-error results within the studied setting, rather than claims of exact prediction indefinitely.
icml-2024-consistent-long-term-forecasti.tldr: Improved operator estimators provide forecasting-error guarantees uniform over time, including infinite horizons, for the studied ergodic dynamical systems.

paragraphs: Neural recordings often contain recurring patterns that involve both which neurons fire and when they fire. Such spontaneous activity is relevant to memory, learning, and navigation, but detecting repeated sequences becomes challenging as recordings grow. This paper focuses on making that detection efficient enough to analyze large collections of neural spike data.

The proposed method, convSeq, learns spatiotemporal filters through backpropagation. These filters identify patterns distributed across neurons and time. Because the method is unsupervised, its task is to discover recurring structure in the recordings without requiring supplied labels for the sequences. Learning the filters provides a way to adapt pattern detection to the observed activity.

The authors evaluate convSeq on synthetic data and real neural recordings, reporting substantially greater speed than existing methods alongside strong scalability and efficiency. The findings support its usefulness as an analysis tool for detecting spike sequences. The broader scientific promise is that easier analysis of large recordings could help researchers investigate information processing in neural circuits; that downstream understanding remains a potential consequence.
icml-2024-convseq-fast-and-scalable-meth.tldr: convSeq learns spatiotemporal filters to discover repeating neural spike patterns, with substantially improved speed and scalability in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: ELF aims to represent a speaker’s overall vocal characteristics in detail without additional training on that target speaker’s dataset. The motivation is a gap between methods designed to handle new speakers and models trained specifically to synthesize speech from multiple known speakers. The paper seeks a representation that can support detailed voice characteristics even for unseen speakers.

The method learns speech features, discretizes them, and uses the resulting representation to condition a speech-synthesis model. This places the speaker’s characteristics in an encoded form that the synthesizer can use. The authors also investigate whether those features contain enough information to reconstruct the original speaker’s speech and whether they can support newly created artificial speakers.

Subjective evaluations report higher speaker-similarity scores for unseen speakers than for seen speakers of a high-performance multispeaker model, as well as substantial gains over a zero-shot method. The paper also reports strong artificial-speaker generation and complete reconstruction of original speech from the encoded features. These findings motivate a possible broader role for the representation in encoding and reconstructing speaker characteristics.
icml-2024-elf-encoding-speaker-specific-.tldr: ELF encodes speaker characteristics into discrete speech features, reporting strong unseen-speaker similarity without additional target-speaker training.

paragraphs: When several probability distributions describe reference data, combining them may require an average distribution rather than an average of individual numbers. This paper studies the Wasserstein barycenter, an averaging concept grounded in optimal transport. The objective is to aggregate reference distributions in a way that reflects the cost of transporting probability mass between them.

The proposed method builds on the dual formulation of optimal transport and a neural optimal-transport solver. Its adversarial learning objective has two optimization levels and supports general cost functions. These features distinguish it from typical adversarial approaches to barycenters that use three optimization levels and concentrate primarily on quadratic costs.

The authors establish theoretical error bounds and demonstrate the approach in illustrative examples and image-data settings. The contribution therefore combines a scalable computational formulation with analysis of its error. Supporting broader costs makes the averaging procedure more flexible about how differences between distributions are measured, while the two-level objective simplifies the optimization structure relative to the approaches described in the abstract.
icml-2024-estimating-barycenters-of-dist.tldr: A neural optimal-transport method estimates Wasserstein barycenters using two-level adversarial optimization, general costs, and theoretical error bounds.

paragraphs: Molecular interactions involve objects represented at different levels of detail, such as proteins and small molecules. Using separate encoders for each molecular type can make it difficult to learn the interaction physics they share. This paper proposes a common representation: describe a three-dimensional molecular complex as a geometric graph whose elements are sets.

The Generalist Equivariant Transformer processes this representation with bilevel attention, feed-forward transformations, and layer normalization. Each module handles sets of varying sizes and is E(3) equivariant, meaning its behavior respects the corresponding transformations of three-dimensional geometry. The architecture aims to capture both molecule-specific hierarchies and physical relationships that apply across molecular types.

A key design claim is that GET retains fine-grained information at every level, unlike conventional hierarchical models based on pooling. Experiments involving proteins, small molecules, RNA, and DNA support its effectiveness and generalization across the evaluated domains. The contribution is a shared geometric modeling framework that accommodates different molecular granularities while maintaining the detailed information needed to describe their interactions.
icml-2024-generalist-equivariant-transfo.tldr: GET uses a shared geometric representation and equivariant transformer to learn interactions across molecular types while retaining fine-grained hierarchical information.

paragraphs: Instrumental-variable regression can be expressed through conditional moment restrictions: relationships that an estimator should satisfy in the data distribution. Many existing estimators approach this by changing the weights assigned to observed samples. With large independent and identically distributed datasets, such reweighting can offer enough flexibility, but it may miss relevant information when observations are corrupted or adversarially altered.

The paper introduces the Sinkhorn Method of Moments, an estimator based on optimal transport. It uses data-derivative information to account for the geometry of the data manifold. This gives the estimation procedure information about the structure around observations, addressing a weakness of approaches whose representation of distributional variation relies on sample reweighting.

The authors provide a simple plug-and-play implementation and report performance comparable to related estimators in standard settings. Under data corruption and adversarial attacks, they report improved robustness. The practical significance is that incorporating geometry can strengthen behavior under problematic data while preserving competitive performance in the ordinary settings examined, without claiming that reweighting methods always fail.
icml-2024-geometry-aware-instrumental-va.tldr: The Sinkhorn Method of Moments incorporates data geometry into instrumental-variable regression, improving reported robustness to corruption and adversarial attacks.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether learning can change how a model learns from later documents. The authors attach random-string tags to text in a synthetic fine-tuning dataset, using those tags as indicators of usefulness. They then examine whether the model subsequently makes greater use of text carrying tags previously associated with useful information.

The experiments find this behavior during further fine-tuning, which the authors call implicit meta-learning. The model has learned a cue that influences later updates, rather than merely using the cue to answer a question in the current context. This supplies a controlled demonstration that document-associated signals can affect how information is incorporated into model parameters.

The phenomenon appears in pretrained language models, models trained from scratch, and a vision task. Larger models and smaller batch sizes tend to exhibit more of it. Probing also examines changes in how knowledge is stored. The findings suggest a possible mechanism for learning to favor reliable sources, while the demonstrated evidence concerns usefulness tags in the studied settings rather than general recognition of real-world source reliability.
icml-2024-implicit-meta-learning-may-lea.tldr: Controlled experiments show that models can learn usefulness tags that influence how strongly they learn from similarly tagged text in later fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning improves a policy using a fixed batch of data when collecting fresh experience is unavailable. A central difficulty is that the learned policy may encounter trajectories distributed differently from those in the batch. Pessimistic penalties account for this mismatch, but existing concentration-bound penalties can be overly conservative in sparse regions and may perform worse than unpenalized alternatives.

The authors derive a new penalty using Stein discrepancy, an evaluable one-sample test that measures a discrepancy between data and the true distribution. The construction requires minimal smoothness conditions and permits mixtures for representing the distribution of next states. This matters because transition outcomes can have multiple modes rather than following a single concentrated pattern.

The resulting information-directed pessimism treats the discrepancy as a measure of the information available in offline data. The paper reports practical performance gains from its discrete Stein-discrepancy penalty and extends prior regret analysis to multimodal distributions. Its contribution combines a different way to quantify mismatch with guarantees accommodating richer transition distributions.
icml-2024-information-directed-pessimism.tldr: Information-directed pessimism uses Stein discrepancy to penalize offline reinforcement-learning uncertainty, with reported performance gains and regret analysis covering multimodal distributions.

paragraphs: Long robotic demonstrations often contain several subtasks requiring different skills. Learning from the entire sequence is difficult without identifying useful intermediate frames and relating them to the skills being performed. KISA addresses these two needs together, using pretrained visual-language representations to decompose demonstrations that lack annotations.

A temporal enhancement module gives each frame’s representation access to a wider span of the video. This helps represent the meaning of changing actions across time. The method then combines coarse contrastive learning with a finer monotonic encouragement mechanism to improve alignment between visual keyframes and language descriptions of skills. The goal is a decomposition whose selected frames have understandable skill associations.

Across three benchmarks, KISA outperforms competitive baselines in both keyframe-identification accuracy and interpretability. The authors also report robust generalization and flexibility in the choice of pretrained representations. These findings support jointly identifying keyframes and annotating skills as a useful way to organize long demonstrations, with temporal context helping connect individual images to the broader action sequence.
icml-2024-kisa-a-unified-keyframe-identi.tldr: KISA jointly identifies keyframes and associates them with skills, improving the reported accuracy and interpretability of long robotic-demonstration decomposition.

paragraphs: Variational logistic regression approximates Bayesian inference by optimizing a tractable distribution in place of the full posterior. A difficulty is that its evidence lower bound contains an intractable expectation. Existing approaches use Monte Carlo sampling, numerical quadrature, or mathematical bounds, with tradeoffs between computational expense and the quality of the resulting posterior approximation.

The paper introduces a new bound for the expected softplus function and applies it to variational logistic regression and Gaussian-process classification. Unlike other bounding approaches, it does not require expanding the variational family or adding parameters specifically to make the bound tight. This keeps the approximation from acquiring those additional modeling or optimization components.

The authors show that their bound is tighter than the state of the art and report state-of-the-art performance for the resulting variational posterior. They also find computation significantly faster than Monte Carlo methods. The contribution targets a specific mathematical bottleneck in Bayesian classification, improving the bound used for inference while supporting both posterior quality and computational efficiency.
icml-2024-logistic-variational-bayes-rev.tldr: A tighter softplus-expectation bound improves variational Bayesian classification without additional variational parameters and computes significantly faster than Monte Carlo methods.

paragraphs: Incremental gradient and shuffled variants of stochastic gradient descent are widely used because they combine practical convergence behavior with efficient data access. Their theoretical behavior is less fully understood for smooth, nonconvex objectives. This paper examines convergence when the training data can be processed in arbitrary orders, providing a broad framework for analyzing these optimization methods.

The main improvements concern incremental gradient and single-shuffle stochastic gradient descent. By allowing arbitrary data ordering in the analysis, the framework addresses how convergence can be justified beyond a narrow choice of ordering. The work strengthens guarantees for these existing methods, focusing on the mathematical account of their progress toward a specified accuracy.

If n denotes the training-set size, the authors improve the optimization term in the convergence guarantee from O(n / epsilon) to O(1 / epsilon). This is an n-fold improvement in that term. Its meaning is a sharper dependence within the bound, not a reported n-fold wall-clock speedup or a claim that every part of the algorithm’s cost becomes independent of dataset size.
icml-2024-on-convergence-of-incremental-.tldr: A convergence analysis improves the optimization term for incremental gradient and single-shuffle SGD by a factor equal to the training-set size.

paragraphs: Planning toward a goal becomes easier when rich observations are represented by compact states. However, a compact representation can omit a crucial relationship: whether one state is reachable from another. This paper argues that representations learned through variational autoencoders or inverse dynamics can miss that relationship, limiting their usefulness for planning and goal-conditioned decision making.

PcLast uses a two-stage approach. It first learns a representation through multistep inverse dynamics to remove distracting information. It then transforms that representation so that reachable states are associated in Euclidean space. The second stage aims to make the geometry of the representation useful for action planning, rather than relying on compactness alone.

Simulation experiments show significant sampling-efficiency improvements in reward-based settings. In reward-free settings, the approach produces layered state abstractions that support computationally efficient hierarchical planning for ad hoc goals with no additional samples. That last result concerns planning using the learned abstractions; the method still learns its representation beforehand. The findings connect planning performance to representing reachability explicitly.
icml-2024-pclast-discovering-plannable-c.tldr: PcLast organizes learned states by reachability, improving sampling efficiency and enabling hierarchical planning for new goals without additional samples.

paragraphs: Private selection mechanisms are building blocks for tasks such as choosing queries, aggregating votes, and tuning hyperparameters under differential privacy. Their usefulness depends partly on how tightly privacy loss can be accounted for. Analyses based on Rényi differential privacy can lose precision when converted to the final epsilon-delta privacy guarantee that an application needs.

This paper works directly with privacy profiles, which describe delta as a function of epsilon. It provides a recipe for bounding the profiles of ReportNoisyMax and PrivateTuning from the profiles of their underlying algorithms. This makes the privacy accounting compositional: information about the component algorithms is used to analyze the larger selection procedure.

Numerical results improve on Rényi-based accounting across all regimes of interest studied, and end-to-end private-learning experiments show substantial benefits. The analysis also suggests alternative distributions for randomizing the number of rounds, including a binomial distribution that gives larger improvements in certain regimes. The contribution combines tighter accounting with guidance about mechanism design, while keeping those extra gains conditional on the regime.
icml-2024-privacy-profiles-for-private-s.tldr: Direct privacy-profile analysis tightens accounting for private selection and tuning, with reported benefits in private learning and certain randomized-round designs.

paragraphs: This paper proposes nonparametric density estimation using a Sobolev-norm regularizer. The regularization makes the model’s preference for particular density shapes explicit and interpretable, and the method is statistically consistent. Although the associated kernel lacks a closed analytic expression, the authors show how to approximate it through sampling.

Fitting the model requires solving a nonconvex optimization problem on which ordinary gradient methods perform poorly. The authors obtain effective solutions by combining an appropriate initialization with natural-gradient optimization. This is a practical part of the contribution: the proposed statistical formulation needs a suitable optimization procedure to produce useful estimates.

The outputs are pre-densities, so they are not guaranteed to integrate to one. That prevents using log-likelihood for cross-validation in the proposed setup. The paper instead adapts score-matching methods based on Fisher divergence for model selection. On the ADBench anomaly-detection suite, the resulting method ranks second among more than fifteen algorithms, providing empirical support for the full combination of regularization, optimization, and validation choices.
icml-2024-sobolev-space-regularised-pre-.tldr: Sobolev-regularized pre-density estimation combines natural gradients and score-based validation, ranking second among more than fifteen methods on ADBench.

paragraphs: For a nonconvex objective, reaching a point with a small gradient does not establish that the point is locally minimizing. Second-order conditions add information about curvature and help rule out strict saddles and other non-minimizing stationary points. This paper asks how computationally difficult it is to find points satisfying approximate second-order conditions.

The main result classifies the problem as PLS-complete, placing it in the same complexity class as finding approximate first-order stationary points. This resolves the question of whether imposing the second-order requirement changes that complexity classification. It does not imply that checking these conditions guarantees a local minimum, a stronger task already known to be NP-hard.

The result also reveals an unusual distinction between constrained and unconstrained domains. Under the conjecture that PLS differs from FNP, finding approximate second-order stationary points is easier in unconstrained domains than in constrained ones. Earlier first-order results give the opposite comparison unless PLS equals CLS. These conditional contrasts show that adding constraints can affect first-order and second-order search problems differently.
icml-2024-the-computational-complexity-o.tldr: Finding approximate second-order stationary points is PLS-complete, matching first-order search and revealing a conditional complexity contrast between constrained and unconstrained domains.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement-learning policies can base decisions on features whose changes are difficult to perceive yet strongly affect the chosen action. This creates a problem for understanding the stability of their decision boundaries. The paper develops a theoretically grounded diagnostic method for analyzing directions in which those boundaries are unstable, across both space and time.

Experiments in the Arcade Learning Environment show that the method identifies correlated directions of instability. It also measures how shifts in samples reshape the sensitive directions of a policy. This provides a structured account of sensitivity, including relationships among unstable directions and changes in those relationships, rather than treating instability as a single aggregate property.

A notable empirical finding concerns robust training. The evaluated state-of-the-art robust training techniques produce disjoint unstable directions with much larger temporal oscillations than standard training. This result complicates the interpretation of robustness in those experiments; it does not establish that robust training is universally inferior. The authors suggest that these diagnostics could help guide the construction of more reliable neural policies.
icml-2024-understanding-and-diagnosing-d.tldr: A policy-sensitivity diagnostic reveals correlated instabilities and finds larger temporal oscillations under the robust training methods evaluated.

paragraphs: Iterative prompting asks a language model to revisit or refine its responses through further prompts. It is tempting to expect that additional rounds will improve an answer, but this paper investigates whether they actually improve truthfulness. The study considers both accuracy and calibration: whether the confidence associated with responses matches how often they are correct.

Experiments compare variants of iterative prompting and find that naive approaches can significantly reduce truthfulness while making calibration errors worse. In the tested settings, prompting the model again is therefore not enough to ensure a more reliable answer. Changes in confidence also matter, because a response can become less trustworthy if its confidence becomes less aligned with its correctness.

The authors introduce several prompting variants designed to address the problems they identify. These variants show marked improvements over existing baselines. The contribution is both diagnostic and constructive: it documents failure modes of naive iteration and demonstrates more promising alternatives. The evidence supports careful design of the prompting procedure, rather than a general guarantee that repeated refinement improves truthfulness.
icml-2024-understanding-the-effects-of-i.tldr: Naive iterative prompting can worsen truthfulness and calibration, while the paper’s redesigned prompting variants improve over evaluated baselines.

paragraphs: VideoPoet investigates how a language-model architecture can generate video from varied conditioning information. It uses a decoder-only transformer that processes images, videos, text, and audio. Bringing these inputs into a shared model allows the video-generation system to respond to several kinds of supplied information within the same architectural framework.

Training follows two stages: pretraining and task-specific adaptation. During pretraining, the model learns from a mixture of multimodal generation objectives within an autoregressive transformer. The pretrained model then serves as a foundation for adaptation to different video-generation tasks. This makes the training mixture central to developing capabilities that can be used across multiple tasks.

The authors report state-of-the-art empirical results in zero-shot video generation, emphasizing the fidelity of generated motion. The stated contribution combines broad multimodal conditioning with a language-model-style training process for video synthesis. The reported zero-shot results sit within a system that also includes task-specific adaptation; the abstract does not present the whole training pipeline as requiring no task-directed training.
icml-2024-videopoet-a-large-language-mod.tldr: VideoPoet uses a multimodal autoregressive transformer for video generation, reporting state-of-the-art zero-shot results with high-fidelity motion.
